A shorter but steeper off-trail alternative climbs from Lake of the Angels (reached via the Putvin Trail), crossing the ridge and dropping into the valley below Mount Stone before climbing the ridge west of Stone toward Hopper.
before.approach: The North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date; check the park's trail conditions before planning. When open, the standard way in starts at the Staircase trailhead (~785 ft) and follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, past Camp Pleasant to Nine Stream Camp, where the trail fords the river (deep and swift in high snowmelt or heavy rain). Above Nine Stream it climbs steeply past Two Bear Camp, brushy between Two Bear and the divide, to First Divide (4,688 ft), about 12.5 miles from the trailhead. The much longer alternative comes up the Duckabush River Trail and climbs over First Divide from the north past Home Sweet Home. Just below First Divide on the Skokomish side, the long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the main trail; its tread has gone under brush, so expect to bushwhack south and east through forest, then climb open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Most parties make it a multi-day trip, camping at Two Bear Camp, First Divide or Home Sweet Home rather than pushing car-to-car.

before.beta: Most parties reach Crescent Lake, which sits below Howard's south side along the Nason Ridge Trail, from either the Merritt Lake Trailhead (shorter, more direct) or the Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock-Crescent col (longer, more scenic, and commonly combined with Rock Mountain). From Crescent Lake's NE side, ascend north up open talus and meadow slopes; the upper mountain narrows into a loose, dirty class 3 gully before easing back to talus and a climbers' trail to the summit. Many parties combine the ascent with a traverse to neighboring Mount Mastiff (about 1 mile away) or Rock Mountain for a full Nason Ridge outing.

before.detailed_rack: Use the full length of a 70m rope if rappelling on a single rope, which is recommended. Bring 16 draws, 2-4 of them alpine. All anchors are bolted and set up for rappel.

before.beta: From High Pass, descend into the basin below the peak. Traverse west and ascend boulder fields and scree to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 feet. Locate the gully system in the rocky face with two narrow channels 30 feet apart; take the right channel and ascend the narrow then open gully to broken rock to attain the ridge top. Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the summit. Most of ridge top has a way trail and the route is partially marked with cairns after leaving the basin, but cairns may be far apart and the way trail may disappear for long stretches. If you lose cairns or way trail most gullies probably work though some may be more difficult than others.

From Flapjack Lakes, either contour around to the right or climb east and then south over the forested ridge to the head of the Madeline Creek basin. Exposed rock scrambling from there gains the north ridge, which leads south to the summit. The 5,700-ft north peak, the prominent point seen from the lakes, is not the top; keep it on your left. Allow about three hours from the lakes. The scrambling is class 3 for most of its length, with a class 4 chockstone move near the summit. The terrain is loose: steep duff and scree below the ridge, the chockstone gully and a boulder field, and an airy knife-edge near the top, so route-finding and care matter as much as difficulty. Most parties camp at the lakes; car-to-car it is a very long day. A different, easier line climbs the ridge south of the peak from lower on the valley trail, but its old trail burned in 1985 and is largely gone.

Approach via Thunder Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass (19.6 mi, 4,900 ft gain from trailhead), then traverse northward 2 miles across heather and alpine meadows to Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Ascend the gentle glacier to the south ridge (Hogsback), negotiate a snow-filled gully through cliff bands, and scramble Class 3-4 rock via ledges on the east side of the summit ridge to the summit.
before.approach: Start at Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR 20 mile 130 (elevation 1,060 ft). Follow Thunder Creek Trail south for approximately 16-18 miles to Thunder Basin camp around 6,000 ft. From Thunder Basin, cross meadows and begin ascending. Traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, gaining approximately 2 miles to reach Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Campsites exist at Thunder Basin and other designated locations along the approach.

before.beta: Approach via Easy Pass (6,500 ft) from Highway 20 mile 151, descend into Fisher Basin, then off-trail climb to Banded Glacier basin. Ascend unstable scree slopes to reach the glacier, cross the Banded Glacier to meet the NE ridge at approximately 8,800 feet, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to the summit. The critical transition point is gaining the NE ridge on solid rock rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. (A longer, always-open alternate approach exists via the Thunder Creek/Fisher Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground — ~13 mi one-way vs. ~10 mi via Easy Pass — useful when Easy Pass Trailhead is gated by SR 20's seasonal closure.)

Approach via Easy Pass (6,500 ft) from Highway 20 mile 151, descend into Fisher Creek valley, cross Fisher Creek, travel up Douglas Creek valley (extremely brushy, slow progress), gain Douglas Glacier basin, ascend steep glacier with steeper ice/snow sections to col, traverse to meet Banded Glacier, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to summit via standard summit block.

An off-trail scramble approached via the Swamp Creek drainage off the Agnes Creek/PCT corridor. From a Swamp Creek camp, travelers cross Swamp Creek, climb through brush and open basin to about 4,000', then work up scree and talus (with lingering snow possible) toward a roughly 7,300' notch on the southwest ridge. From the notch, a traverse below a prominent white vertical rock band on grassy ledges leads to an exposed, narrowing class 3 gully; the final ~200' to the summit climbs through loose, stacked boulders (choss).

Most parties start from the Merritt Lake Trailhead, hike the maintained trail to Merritt Lake, then follow the Nason Ridge Trail for about a mile and turn uphill on an unsigned boot path that climbs steep forest to Mastiff's southeast ridge (other lines reach the peak from the Crescent Lake basin via the Howard-Mastiff ridge, or up the northeast ridge from Lost Lake). On the ridge, follow the crest -- staying just below it to avoid small cliffs and dense subalpine trees -- to the summit. The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake, so navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge. Many parties combine the peak with Mount Howard (1 mile west) as a single long day.
before.approach: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft). Hike the Merritt Lake Trail up toward the ridge, connecting with the Nason Ridge Trail; figure a long day (roughly 10 miles round trip, ~4,900 ft gain for Mastiff alone) or an overnight via Merritt or Lost Lake.

before.beta: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, hike the Royal Basin trail to Royal Lake/Upper Royal Basin, then climb a steep snowfield to the ridge notch (locally called Royal Pass or Deception Pass) dividing Royal and Deception basins. Descend into Deception Basin, cross the stagnant, minimally-crevassed Mystery Glacier to a col (~6,700 ft) on the peak's east side, then work up mixed scree, snow, and rock on the south side of the mountain, finishing with a short, exposed Class 4 breccia section/gully to the summit block.

Mount Olson sees very few ascents. Most parties reach it as a side trip from the long Six Ridge traverse between the South Fork and North Fork Skokomish valleys: hike the South Fork Skokomish River Trail to Sundown Pass/Sundown Lake, join the Six Ridge Trail, then leave it on the primitive, unsigned way trail toward Mount Olson before finishing cross-country to the summit. There is no recorded roped climbing route, rack, or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak anywhere; it is treated purely as a bushwhack/scramble objective by Olympic peak-baggers.

From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the Dingford Creek Trail (multiple creek crossings) toward Hester Lake and Little Hester Lake — roughly the first 5-6 miles. From the lakes basin, ascend the boulder field south of Little Hester Lake to gain Price's east ridge near Point 5,480'/5,440', traverse the steep north side of the ridge to a col around 5,400 ft just east of the true summit, and finish with a short ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit. Expect Class 3 scrambling with occasional steep snow or rock gullies on the ridge, and real routefinding difficulty — at least one party's own GPS track diverged noticeably between ascent and descent.

Undertaken as a link between the two peaks (not from a trailhead) after climbing one via another route. Rahm-to-Custer is the easier direction to routefind: follow the crest (exposed on the north side, easier scrambling on flatter rock) to a notch below Custer's final arête, then find a hidden Class 4 gully roughly 50 ft below and left of the notch to bypass the unfeasible Class 5 arête. Custer-to-Rahm is the harder direction to routefind, since the crux gully is difficult to spot from above.

First skied in 1997 by Armond DuBuque, Doug Ingersoll, Andrew McLean, and Carl Skoog; historically accessed via the Mowich Lake road, which has had no public access since the SR 165 bridge closed in April 2025.
before.approach: From Mowich Lake, hike through Spray Park and up the lower Ptarmigan Ridge to camps near 9,600 ft between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers, then drop to the Edmunds Glacier and the base of the headwall.

before.beta: Grade II-III alpine glacier route. Approach via Westside Road to Tahoma Creek Trail (listed as closed by the park: washed out and exposed to debris flows), ascending Wonderland Trail to ~5,600 ft, then climbing southern side of glacier with multiple diagonal traverses.

Mixed alpine terrain requiring pins, screws, nuts, and cams; multiple lines/linkups exist (e.g., the East Rib, and 'Traverse of the Angels' style link-ups), but the wall as a whole is rarely climbed given the objective danger.

From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100 ft), follow the Snow Lake Trail past Snow Lake to Gem Lake, then leave the maintained trail and traverse southwest up the ridge toward the peak. A cairn-marked traverse below cliffs near 5,400 ft leads into a small basin below the summit block, from which a class 2-3 gully of steep dirt and heather (often partly snow-filled) gains the final ~400+ ft to the 5,835 ft summit. Round trip is roughly 13 miles with about 2,700 ft of gain, commonly taking around 7 hours car-to-car; the crux is route-finding on the cairned traverse and footing in the gully when wet or snow-covered.

The standard/easiest and most commonly climbed route on Sefrit. From Ruth Creek, climbers cross the creek and bushwhack up through slide alder to the base of the 'Wall Street' couloir, a roughly 1,500-vertical-foot snow gully about 50 feet wide at 30-35 degrees. The couloir tops out on the Northwest Glacier at about 5,000 ft, crossed (roped, with pickets/flukes for crevasse hazard) to a broad saddle at 6,500 ft just west of the summit. From the saddle, parties either climb a steep, narrow chute due south to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle, or traverse southeast across a shallow snow bowl beneath the summit — the traverse exposes climbers to cornices and is usually roped with snow protection. The route finishes on the southeast ridge: a straightforward Class 2 scramble broken by about 100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle. routeFt here (3,691 ft) is a computed total combining the couloir, glacier crossing, and final ridge scramble, since no aggregate route length is known.

Via North Face approach or from Fisher Chimneys route (drop down White Salmon Glacier approximately 1,000 feet). Cross the NW Rib route to gain Hanging Glacier. Features nice mix of glacier travel and ice climbing up to 65 degrees. Connected to Crystal Glacier at upper margins.

From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road, the Putvin Trail climbs about 3,400 ft in roughly 3.5 miles to Lake of the Angels, including a very steep, sometimes near-vertical headwall requiring hand-and-foot scrambling on roots and rock. Beyond the lake, skirt the north/west shore and climb alpine slopes and a scree-and-snow gully (climber's-right gully) to a roughly 5,800 ft saddle at the peak's northeast/east side. From the saddle, cross scree, grass, and rock slopes southwest and scramble the southeast slope/south ridge on generally rotten, loose rock (Class 2, locally 3 to 3+) to the summit. The route has three summit horns; parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true (south) high point. Snow lingers on the gully and saddle well into summer and is reported as firm/frail, so an ice axe is commonly carried into July.

Classed as advanced scrambling with glacier travel followed by a short Class 4 rock step. Parties rope up for the glaciated section (crevasses and a bergschrund are noted) and carry a small rock rack/runners for the final step, which is on loose, lichen-covered rock. It can be approached from a camp at Silver Lake (via Silver Creek) or from Ouzel Lake (via Depot Creek and over the Custer-Spickard saddle).

From Marmot Lake Camp (~4,400 ft) leave the maintained trail and follow a small creek up into an amphitheater on the west side of the peak; easy Class 1 slopes lead from the amphitheater to the summit. The multi-day approach up the Duckabush valley (roughly 21-23 trail miles one-way to Marmot Lake) is the real crux of the trip, not the summit scramble itself. An alternate approach from the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish side reaches First Divide, drops into a basin with an unnamed lake, and climbs the saddle between Mount Duckabush and Mount Steel before turning north along the ridge to the summit block; the park lists that trail closed between the Staircase Rapids Loop and Home Sweet Home since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, which leaves the Duckabush/Marmot Lake line as the open approach.

Popular with scramblers and trail runners seeking a harder version of the peak. Features Class 2-3 rock steps, steep root/dirt tread, and minor exposure, with lingering snow near the ridge crest into early summer. Many parties ascend via Kamikaze and descend the standard trail through Rachor Pass to make a ~10-mile loop rather than retracing the steep boot track.

From the Upper Trailhead the trail switchbacks up through old-growth hemlock/fir with a rhododendron understory, crosses a couple of seasonal streams in the first 1.5 miles, then eases into ridge walking with early views. Around 2.5 miles it reaches Camp Windy/Windy Lake amid wildflower meadows, then climbs a final steady, switchbacked pitch above treeline to the open, windswept summit plateau. The Lower Trailhead adds about 2 extra round-trip miles and roughly 500 extra feet of gain via the same trail corridor. There is no scrambling or hands-on terrain on the standard route; the only technical consideration is wind/weather exposure once above Camp Windy.
before.approach: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded old-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water). At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.6 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1 mile to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing.

before.beta: The Northeast Ridge is the one genuinely 'moderate' way up an otherwise defended peak. From a col/bivy site above Thornton Lakes, the route crosses a shrinking glacier remnant and a loose gully to gain the ridge crest, then follows roughly 9-12 belayed pitches (mostly easy 5th class, with a runout 5.6 traverse and the signature 5.7 offwidth crux) plus short simul-climbed/scrambled sections along an exposed, towered ridge to the summit. The descent reverses the ridge with a long series of rappels and downclimbing back to the col.

From a base camp or day-hike start at Watson Lakes, leave the maintained trail and work up open slopes on the mountain's north side toward the notch between the lower East Peak and the true (western) summit. Cross a short but steep snow finger / remnant glacier apron in the notch (ice axe and crampons or microspikes advisable for most of the season), then scramble loose, mossy class 3 terrain west along the south side of the ridge and along a narrow, knife-edge ridge crest to the true summit. Most parties descend the same way; some instead drop east onto the shrinking Watson Glacier to shortcut back toward the lakes.
before.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line in its entirety — this is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the exposed, narrow class 2-3 summit ridge (many parties use a hand line here) back down the short loose gully to the base of the summit block, then traverse back around the block and along the ridge to the 5,900-ft saddle. From the saddle, descend the east gully (the same talus/snow line used on the way up — avoid the west gully's moat/snow-bridge hazard) back into the basin above Watson Lakes, then pick up the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 at the lakes for the hike out to the trailhead, passing back through the two junctions (the ~4,700-ft Anderson/Watson Lakes fork, then the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 junction at 1 mile from the trailhead). Descent times are typically close to ascent times (roughly 3+ hours from summit to car), consistent with a straightforward if loose reversal. Descent-specific hazards: loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle, glissade/postholing risk on residual snow into midsummer, rotten moats/snow bridges if the west-side line is mistakenly used, and route-finding across the open, unmarked basin and ridge in flat light or fog — the exposed summit-ridge downclimb remains the technical crux in both directions.

before.beta: From the Tubal Cain Trailhead, a well-graded trail leads about 6 miles to Buckhorn Lake, the last water source and jumping-off point for the summit. Above the lake the route leaves the trail, climbing through avalanche-damaged timber to treeline near 5,800 ft, then ascending loose scree and talus -- either angling toward the roughly 6,420-ft saddle between Iron Mountain and Worthington, or straight up a wide gully south of the lake -- to the peak's open summit plateau. A final short scramble up a rock fin, with some exposure, gains the true summit. Overall the route is Class 2 with a Class 3 summit block, but loose rock and off-trail routefinding make it feel harder than the grade suggests to many parties.

Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Parties reach it either by continuing the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past the summit and along the connecting ridge/snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or from the south on the longer Green Mountain–Mount Misch–Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mutchler. Terrain is a mix of steep heather, talus, snow/glacier remnants, and low-class rock; one documented traverse rappelled over a cornice to reach the peak.
before.approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; no published figure gives the car-to-summit distance for Mutchler itself, but Snowking, reached by the same approach over Kindy Ridge, is roughly 16-18 miles round trip. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.

before.beta: From the Cedar Creek Trail, parties leave the trail to bushwhack toward Cedar Creek, ford it (difficulty varies greatly with flow — see Watch Out), and continue cross-country along/above the Shelokum Creek drainage to open terrain below a broad, moderately angled northwest couloir. The couloir has been climbed on foot (crampons) and descended on skis; above the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of dry, loose talus on the north ridge leads to the summit. A 2024 ascent found the snow "shockingly icy" and bypassed part of the slope by dropping right onto loose rock and scree.

First recorded climbed by Mark Bebie on September 7, 1986, who reached it by descending a couloir onto an unnamed glacier north of Primus (accessed from the North Klawatti Glacier after climbing Austera Peak the same day) and traversing to the ridge's base. The ridge took about an hour to climb once gained. It is very rarely repeated and only lightly documented; other parties have approached instead from McAllister Camp via Tricouni Peak's lower north ridge, or via a north-south Primus-Eldorado glacier traverse.
before.approach: Same Thunder Creek Trailhead approach as the East Slope route (Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, about 6 miles up the Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy at ~6,000 ft near the toe of the Borealis Glacier) — the North Ridge is reached by traversing around the lake instead of climbing the glacier from camp.

before.beta: The North Ridge - West Side is one of the primary technical routes on Molar Tooth. The route ascends via the west rib with multiple short low 5th class pitches (up to 5.4), solid granite with vertical jointing, though protection is spaced in places, and enjoyable alpine climbing despite loose rock concerns. The descent via north ridge rappels requires careful anchor placement and rope management due to potential loose rock.

A ridge-crest link between Cloudy Peak and North Star: from Cloudy Pass, scramble the ridge up to Cloudy Peak with expanding views toward Glacier Peak, Eldorado, and Buckner, on rock that is reasonably solid Class 4 with an option to keep it at Class 3. From Cloudy Peak, lose elevation and cross talus slopes to reach North Star, finishing on the same lichen-slicked Class 3-4 summit step as the standard route. Most parties descend directly toward the Cloudy Pass Trail (rejoining it around 6,300 ft) rather than re-climbing Cloudy Peak.

The West Ridge is the standard and by far the most popular route on North Twin Sister. After a long logging-road and trail approach to treeline near Dailey Prairie, the route follows the ridge crest (keeping to climber's right of the crest on the lower ridge and moving to climber's left near the false summits, to avoid the hardest moves) past two named rock features — the 'Obelisk' and the 'Cockscomb' — with a notch around 6,300 ft that bypasses a cliff band where the crest is blocked. Most of the climbing is class 3 on excellent, high-friction rock with frequent holds; a handful of class 4 (and, on the crest itself, occasional class 5) moves are encountered, and some parties rope up for a short M1b mixed step on a variation start. Multiple false summits complicate routefinding near the top. Descent is either back down the ridge or, early season, a steep glissade down snow on the north face.

Grade: 5.7+ YDS, Grade IV, 12 pitches, 4,000 feet. First ascent: 1963. Route: Climb partway up C-J couloir to hanging glacier on right; ascend leftmost rib to summit. Hazards: Objective danger from falling rock/ice, steep snow, exposed scrambling, avalanche potential. Equipment: Small-to-medium alpine rock rack (to 3 inches), 10+ runners, helmet. Best season: July-September. No bush climbing.

The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. Descent from the summit was a single 25 m rappel off an anchor down the east side, then scrambling talus around to the south saddle and back past Jabberwocky Tower to Colchuck Lake. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, though not necessarily by this line.

From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~5.4 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.

Approach via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhack to Overcoat Lake basecamp and contour to the Overcoat Glacier. Ascend the glacier, navigate crevasses and moats, then climb the exposed fourth class rock on the northeast side of the summit pyramid. Crampons and ice tools are essential. Descent is via downclimbing and rappels to return to the glacier.
before.approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above about 6,600 ft the route alternates between rock and snow, with one sloping, exposed rock step that requires care to downclimb onto steep snow. A common camp is on rock slabs/benches around 6,600 ft directly overlooking the Overcoat Glacier, roughly 100 ft below the glacier's toe. Total trailhead-to-camp distance is on the order of 15-16 miles with 5,000+ ft of gain; this is a serious, mostly off-trail approach through wilderness terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness) with real route-finding, so a GPS track or careful map work for the Valley of the Chiefs and glacier-bench section is worthwhile. From camp, traverse west across the mellow lower-angle part of the Overcoat Glacier to reach the base of a snow finger on the peak's north/east side that leads to the summit rock.

before.beta: From the summit of Painted Mountain, follow the crest east over broken ridge and snowfields to Magenta Peak. The section from Magenta to Black Mountain is the crux: the ridge is cut by numerous gendarmes that push you off the crest to find bypasses, with at least one awkward mossy downclimb. Black Mountain, the high point of the route, has several ways up: loose scree gullies on its southeast side; a steep heather chute from the basin on its south side to a small col just west of the summit block, then a short, exposed class 3 scramble up the northwest ridge; or, harder, a class 4 corner with slabby footholds on the north side. Descend Black's south side, over lingering snow early in the season, into the basin below it toward Brown Peak, whose summit can be skipped by crossing its shoulder. Continue south to the base of Skullcap Peak and tag it, then follow easier ridge with decent use paths over the Purple Peak area to Portal Peak. Drop to Red Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and follow the crest to White Mountain, whose south ridge has a climber's path. Descend to White Pass.

Opens with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system with finger cracks, crosses right below a roof into a splitter crack to a mid-route ledge, then a second roof leads to a hand crack and stemming corners with a hard exit, topping out via a deep summit chimney; protection is cams and nuts to 3 inches throughout.

A granite ridge climb with lichened overlaps, gardened dirt-filled cracks and clean tactile smears on low-angle granite; the crux comes late, on pitch 9, with an S-curved crack and bulge with smearing moves to chain anchors. Modern bolted anchors added in 2023 made the route rappel-able for the first time.

From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. No rappels are needed — parties walk off. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.

Approach via Pacific Crest Trail north from Exit 52, following Commonwealth Creek trail to the base of the mountain. The final 1,000-1,100 feet ascends the west-facing slope at 30-40 degrees inclination. Most loose rock has been removed by frequent traffic. South-facing sections feature more solid red volcanic slabs. Winter ascents are possible with snow coverage on the southwest ridge when avalanche conditions are stable.
5 bolts to chains. Approach to Megadike North 1.1-1.2 miles past Middle Point Ridge Trailhead.

Parties typically approach via Twisp River Road to either the Reynolds Creek drainage (shortest, most direct) or the Williams Creek trail, then climb open basins and snowfields on the southeast side of the peak to a saddle/notch below the summit. From there, a Class 2-3 gully leads to the ridge crest, followed by a short, somewhat exposed Class 3 scramble on solid granite to the true (southeast) summit. Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin ('the back way'), but all eventually join the same southeast-side summit scramble rather than offering a genuinely distinct technical line.
before.approach: From the Reynolds Creek Trailhead (~3,100–3,170 ft, reached via Forest Road 4435, which crosses the Twisp River near Mystery Campground before the Spur 4435-015 turnoff to the trailhead), the route follows Reynolds Creek Trail #402, an unmaintained, primitive Forest Service trail entering the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. Trail #402 climbs steadily through mixed conifer forest along Reynolds Creek for roughly 3 miles to the confluence where the South Fork of Reynolds Creek meets the main creek (approx. 4,800–5,000 ft) — parties describe scooting across a downed log to make this crossing, which can be a genuine ford in high early-season flow. This confluence is the last reliable, easy water source before the upper basin, so fill up here. Beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread and follow the South Fork drainage, staying roughly 50 ft above the creek to avoid the worst brush and log-hopping directly in the streambed. Expect about 2 miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber, and a boot-path/game-trail tread that comes and goes — this is the route-finding crux of the approach, and parties specifically flag the numerous fallen logs and dense brush here. The drainage opens into a broad talus/scree basin around 5,500–5,700 ft directly below Reynolds Peak's southeast face and the gully/snowfield leading to its east ridge. This basin and the gully above it hold snow well into summer in most years, so carry an ice axe (and traction in early season) even on an otherwise dry-looking late-summer day. From the basin, ascend the scree, talus, and (seasonally) snow of the SE slopes/gully to a saddle/notch on the peak's east ridge, then finish with a short, exposed class 2–3 scramble (occasionally reported as harder, class 3–4, depending on snow coverage) up sound granite summit rocks to the 8,517 ft high point. An alternate, more scenic but similarly long approach exists via Williams Creek Trail and War Creek Ridge from a different Twisp River Road trailhead, but Reynolds Creek Trail #402 is the standard, shorter line. The longer Williams Creek/War Creek Ridge alternative can be combined into a loop with Abernathy Peak or Twisp Pass, running roughly 24 miles round trip with about 8,300 ft of cumulative gain.

before.detailed_rack: A modest rock climbing rack is essential due to poor anchor placements throughout. Bring 1-2 sets of small cams (0.4-1.5 inches) and a set of nuts for protection and rappel anchors. Many parties report difficulty finding solid rock for gear placement; natural features (trees, rocks) may be used for anchors where possible.

before.beta: Climbs the middle of Roan Wall via a 5.8 bolted slab approach pitch, a 5.4 approach pitch, sustained 5.9-5.10 edge and face pitches, and a 5.11a crux slab pitch (P7), finishing with mixed 5.9-5.10- climbing. All belays feature brand-new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors. An enormously overhung boulder (Martha's Place) sits near the base and offers a good camp/bivy spot.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

before.beta: Shares its approach and lower access with Center Stage; before reaching Center Stage's start, traverse about 200 feet right to a pale/white slab between two obvious left-facing corners. Features a pale slab approach pitch, face pitches with friction cruxes, corner climbing, sustained slab sections with crimpy holds, and finishes on a unique pitch combining an overlap crack with low-angle face climbing. Climbs the same very high-quality granite as the rest of Roan Wall.
before.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.

before.beta: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Robinson Creek Trail north, cross Beauty Creek, and turn uphill onto the unmarked, unmaintained Beauty Creek Trail. Climb the brushy, steep Beauty Creek valley, cross a tributary around 5,200-5,260 ft, then ascend open meadow/scree to a small tarn at roughly 6,750-6,800 ft in a rocky basin. From the tarn, climb the loose scree slope (snow-covered in early season) north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge, then turn left (north-west) and follow the ridge about a mile over several false summits — mostly class 2 walking with a few class 3 sections and a narrow, exposed crux just below the true summit.

The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling), then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exit on the standard Rock Mountain Trail. Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).

Park at a turnout across from a large boulder field on the northwest side of the mountain. Climb steeply up the hillside left (east) of the boulder field to gain the northwest ridge, follow it over Point 6315', transition onto the west ridge around 5,400 ft, and finish with a scramble up the summit ridge. In snow season, cliff bands along the ridge are typically turned via snow ramps.

Approach via the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail to Hannegan Pass, then follow an unmaintained climbers' trail south onto the Ruth Glacier and up easy snow to Ruth Mountain's summit. From Ruth, descend about 1,600 ft in two roughly 800-ft steps to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy, cross talus and glacier to a notch west of Icy's Northwest Spire near 6,500 ft, then climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd-3rd class terrain and a short 4th class summit gully to Icy Peak. The whole traverse is reversed to descend.

Boston Basin approach is steeper and rougher than Cascade Pass route. Trail is eroded and steep. Boston Basin sees less traffic and wider crevasse field on Quien Sabe Glacier compared to Sahale Glacier. Ascend left (north) side of Quien Sabe Glacier, watching for crevasses and selecting reasonable line—usually near center in steeper sections. Route between Sahale and Boston Peak summits (Sharkfin Tower is visible reference). Traverse south via col below the two peaks to reach Boston-Sahale Col. From col, traverse exposed snow to reach loose Class 3 summit scramble with persistent cornice into early summer. Final scramble is brief and loose.

Descend exactly the way you went up (a bit of temporary flagging can help on the brushy class 3-4 terrain so you don't wander off-line), and do not reuse any old rappel webbing/tat found at the notch since it's likely to be years old — bring your own to replace it.
before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: descend the northeast ridge back toward the notch/saddle below the true summit, then downclimb or rappel the short class 3/4 technical step just below the summit. Most parties rappel this step — a single 150 ft rope covers both the lead and the rappel, and the rappel itself is short, roughly 50-60 ft. This is a single rappel; no additional roped descents are reported lower on the route. Because Sheep Gap Mountain is an obscure, lightly-visited summit, no fixed bolted anchor is documented — expect to build or use a natural anchor (rock horn, chockstone, or sling around a block) rather than find bolts or chains, and bring gear/webbing to back it up or replace tat. From the base of the rappel, reverse the traverse back to Weden Pass, then retrace the talus/heather traverse and boot path down to Foggy Lake/Gothic Basin, and follow Weden Creek Trail #724 back down to Monte Cristo Road and Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock on the class 3/4 terrain above and below the rappel and re-ford Weden Creek on the way out.

before.beta: From the col between Mount Stuart and Sherpa Peak, ascend the ridge generally trending climber's left. With a 60m rope you can reach the first belay in a cave-like feature with a platform large enough for several climbers; the crux is the crack leading out of the cave (rated 5.4-5.5). A second pitch leads to another anchor, after which a short 4th-class scramble gains the notoriously airy summit block. Descent is about four rappels down the ascent line, three single-rope and a final double-rope rappel to the west notch.

From a col south of Sinister, descend onto the Chickamin Glacier and traverse to the base of the north face at its lowest point. Climb a direct line up the consistent 45-50 degree névé and ice, deviating only briefly to skirt the bergschrund, until the angle eases near the top and a short rock/snow scramble leads to the summit.

From the Stevens Pass parking area, a route climbs past a small gray WSDOT building, under powerlines, and up a gated gravel road to Skyline Lake, then ascends northwest through timber and open slopes to a gap in the Skyline Ridge crest before following the ridge, traversing below rocky sub-points, to the summit. A faint climbers' path parallels much of the gravel-road approach and is faster than the road.

From the Snow Lake trailhead at Alpental, find an unsigned boot path just off an old dirt road. The path climbs a steep, loose creek bed through forest for about a mile to a junction (right forks to Guye Peak/Cave Ridge; stay left/straight for the summit). Continue past a roughly 50-ft waterfall to an open meadow between Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, then switchback up open southwest-facing slopes to the summit. Most parties treat it as a there-and-back half-day trip; it is popular as both a snow-free scramble and, with an ice axe/crampons, a winter/spring snow climb.

From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead, hike the well-worn trail to Pyramid Lake (~2 mi), then follow a steep, less-traveled climbers' trail up the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak into alpine terrain. Traverse south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump onto the Colonial Glacier, climb ~30-degree snow to the Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,840 ft), then descend roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier. Rope up and cross the Neve — parties describe the cleanest line through the center of its crevasse field — to the ridge near The Horseman on Snowfield's west side (~7,700 ft), then finish with roughly 400-600 ft of class 3-4 (occasionally class 5 on variant lines) rock scrambling to the summit.

before.detailed_rack: Pickets and slings for the glacier; minimal rock gear needed.

before.beta: From Edward Mesa (the 'Lost World Plateau'), descend to the south side of the peak to a steep gully marked by a giant chockstone. Pitch 1 climbs 15 feet of 5.7 to a tree; subsequent pitches traverse ledges, include a chimney with a 5.6 downclimb, a 5.7 flake with stemming, and scrambling through boulders and trees to the top.

5.8 YDS / VI- UIAA Grade II Alpine. 5 pitches trad climbing with 4–5 technical pitches. Two 20–30 ft sections of 5.7; extensive 4th–5th class scrambling. Hazards: frequent rockfall, loose rock/choss, exposure, early-season snow/ice. Requires cams, stoppers, long slings. Best June–August (peak July); avoid late season. First Ascent: Myhre & Sorenson (1966).

Grade 5.3-5.7, II-III Alpine. 600 vertical feet over 6 pitches from ridge base to summit. Rock quality excellent. Primary hazards: high exposure, significant glacier crevasses, late-season ice conditions, Class 4 downclimbing. 60m rope required for descent rappels. Accessible via Sulphide Glacier or Fisher Chimneys approaches. Often requires bivy camp due to multi-day approach.
before.detailed_rack: A light trad rack suffices: double-length slings for the ridge, small-to-medium nuts and cams to about 1.5 inches (tricams work well), plus full glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach.

before.beta: A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit, reached via a long glaciated approach from the Eldorado trailhead.

Hike the Sunrise Mine Trail from its trailhead through Wirtz Basin to Headlee Pass, traverse below Sperry's south ridge past Lake Elan (Vesper Lake), then scramble up slabs to the broad saddle between Sperry and Vesper Peaks. From the saddle, follow the west ridge/west slope upward -- easy at first, but above a down-sloping talus and heather bench the route steepens and the exposure increases into sustained Class 3-4 terrain to the summit. Many parties combine Sperry with adjacent Vesper Peak from the same saddle in one long day.

Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge. The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.

The south face is accessed from Spire Col at 7,760 feet. Route climbs class 2-3 scrambling to a class 4 chimney, then traverses class 3 ledges on the southeast face. Final pitch involves friction slab climbing (class 5.6) or alternate cracks left of the slab. Route-finding to the crux can be challenging. The summit horn is extremely exposed with only room for one person at a time; rope belays required for final exposed sections. Descent via two 60-meter rappels to scree.

Approach the peak from Park Creek campground by ascending a loose talus slope, bearing left toward a cirque below the towers. Route-finding requires staying on the correct gully (right-side route preferred over left). Traverse a ledge across the backside of the southern tower with Class 3-4 moves and occasional exposure. Navigate a slight overhang with a squeeze-through section (Class 3), then traverse the summit tower's backside to a small spur. Final approach involves either climbing a 15-foot Class 4 solid face or wrapping around the left side on Class 3 blocks to reach the summit register. Slings are in place near the summit for rappel anchors.

From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, hike the Royal Creek/Upper Dungeness Trail through Royal Basin, continue past Royal Lake into Upper Royal Basin, then leave the maintained trail and travel cross-country to the base of Sundial's east/northeast face. Ascend broken rock and ledges (loose throughout) toward the summit ridge; route-finding is the crux — at least one spot appears to cliff out but a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner allows passage. Continue Class 3 scrambling to the summit.

From Barclay Lake Trailhead, walk a quarter mile back down the road to a spur road, cross Barclay Creek and climb the Tailgunner Creek drainage/couloir to Tailgunner Pass (~5,320 ft), a broad saddle between Gunn Peak's ridge and Tailgunner. From the pass, scramble up Tailgunner's west ridge and south-facing scree/rock slopes to the summit dome; a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers. In late-spring snow conditions parties have instead cramponed up a north-slope snow route and surmounted a corniced west-ridge headwall — a more technical, roped variation not represented by the Class 3 rating.

Approach via the Honeycomb Glacier — either descending from a high camp on Kololo Peaks or traversing in from the White River side over the PCT/Whitechuck and Suiattle Glaciers — to a col west of Tenpeak, then cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier and traverse to the couloir's base. Climb the roughly 1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree couloir (crampons and ice axe, or ski crampons for splitboard/ski parties), then scramble to the NW Ridge where one 5.4 rock pitch leads to the summit.

From Thunder Basin at 5,180 feet, ascend snowfields and rocky slopes toward the summit block. The final two pitches involve Class 4 scrambling up a gully left of the summit col (approximately 85 feet to a ledge), followed by a longer pitch up a face toward a broken chimney containing a good jam crack that leads directly to the summit. Crampons and ice axe essential for snowfield sections. A fixed pin exists for rappel descent assistance. The route sees minimal traffic and requires solid route-finding skills.
before.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb (or rappel, if wet/loose) the broken chimney/face and gully back to the col, then descend the snow/talus back into Thunder Basin. From Thunder Basin, retrace the sheep trail down to the White River Trail junction and hike out to the trailhead. There are no fixed anchors reported on the gully/chimney — parties needing to rappel use natural anchors (horns, chockstones) and should carry extra webbing/cord.

before.beta: A long, mostly non-technical mountaineering route that is more of a route-finding and stamina challenge than a climbing one. From the Lena Lake Trailhead, hike past Lena Lake and through the Valley of the Silent Men to a base-camp area near where the trail meets Lena Creek's forks. From there, climbers' paths lead up the creek drainage to a broad avalanche slope/meadow below the first cliff band; cross this and enter the couloir (snow- or rock-filled depending on season), following it up through the narrow "Hourglass" constriction near ~5,800 ft. Above the Hourglass the couloir broadens; work up and right, staying on firmer rock, then trend back left/up through loose scree to the summit. Early/mid-season the couloir holds continuous snow (ice axe and crampons required, with snow up to 40-45 degrees); by late summer it is a loose, snow-free scree-and-rock scramble.

Above Flapjack Lakes, the standard approach leaves the Gladys Divide trail at about 4,400 ft, short of the divide near a small pond, and climbs an open snow/rock slope southeast toward Sawtooth Pass - snow lingers on it into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. Below the pass, traverse right on loose, exposed class 3-4 ground under the west face of The Fin to the notch south of The Horn. Do not underestimate The Horn as a simple scramble: despite the modest 5.5 grade, the final summit pitch is run-out and the rock demands careful gear placement.
before.approach: Drive Hwy 101 to Hoodsport, then SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road, becomes FR-24 past the lake) roughly 9 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station/trailhead (~800 ft) in the SE corner of Olympic National Park. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4 miles to the Spike Camp junction, then climb steeply another ~3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes (~4,000 ft, 8 miles from the trailhead) — a limited-entry wilderness camping zone, so reserve a permit well ahead. From Flapjack Lakes, follow the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft, then leave it and climb cross-country southeast toward Sawtooth Pass to reach the base of The Fin and The Horn. Round-trip approach mileage to Gladys Divide alone runs close to 19 miles with roughly 4,000+ ft of net gain, before the additional ridge travel and the climb itself — this is realistically a backpack-in with a high camp, not a day trip from the road.

before.beta: A crux start on below-average rock quality for Keechelus, then the route is basically over. Also toprope-able by walking up, but the anchor ledge is slanting and dirty — use a personal anchor system (PAS) when clipping in.

The East Ridge route involves vertical to overhanging rock on pitons to avoid a loose gully below, followed by approximately half a mile of alpine ridge climbing. The route was established as a first ascent during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse in July 2003. Access is gained via a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.
before.approach: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead off the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) near Newhalem, follow the Goodell Creek climbers' path, crossing two branches of the creek before a steep, cairned ascent (roughly 4 miles in) into the Terror Creek drainage. From there, either climb the steep Terror Basin route (about 2.5 miles, ~4,700 ft gain, faint tread, dense brush, and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band) or take the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line to reach a high camp below The Rake's east ridge. Expect a long, unmarked, bushwhack-heavy day-plus approach typical of the Pickets — there is no maintained trail.

before.beta: Parties approach via the Snow Lakes Trail into the Core Enchantments basin, then leave the trail to ascend talus and granite buttresses on Temple's south side. The line climbs mostly class 3-4 terrain - slabs, ledges, and blocky ribs - with exposure increasing near the top, finishing with a short low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) section through a ramp/notch onto the small, airy summit. A helmet and a light rack are commonly carried for the final moves; most parties descend by rappelling and downclimbing the route.

From the Mineral Creek Trailhead, the route follows the Mineral Creek trail before heading off-trail through brush to the base of a long talus slope on Middle Peak's south side. The talus steepens toward the Main-Middle notch, which is marked by a chockstone; from there the line traverses a broad south-facing ledge to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit, then climbs a solid, enjoyable class 4 chimney directly to the top.

Seven-pitch, 800-ft Grade IV 5.12a on the east side of the tower. The route alternates bolt-protected technical slab pitches (P1, P2, P5) with crack pitches (P3, P4, P6-P7) that need a full trad rack. Rock quality is noted as inconsistent, with looser sections on P1 and the P4 roof traverse. Descent is either a rappel of the route with two 70m ropes, or an exposed 4th-class traverse west from the East Shoulder to the same gully used by East Face parties.

From Burgundy Col, descend around the north face to a twin-crack system with obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up (Action Potential's start is roughly 15 ft to the left). Eight pitches climb twin cracks, a chimney/right-facing corner, delicate face moves, and a bulging, thin-corner roof-traverse crux (P4, 5.11a) before wide cracks and chimneys and a final hand-crack/offwidth pitch reach the summit. Described by climbers as a good route that would be excellent with more traffic; some sections (notably the P6 corner) were noted as lichen-covered/dirty as of a 2018 ascent.

Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—sustained, largely overhanging climbing, with most pitches at 5.11–5.12 and several at 5.10. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include the crux 5.12 pitch out a huge roof (pitch 11), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. The approach involves 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab climbing with fixed lines and bolts. Published pitch counts vary between 14 and 20 depending on how the climbing is split or linked; the pitch-by-pitch breakdown here uses the 14-pitch convention.

This is the standard line up the ridge's true high point, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Herb Staley in 1952. From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class rock to a notch on the north side of the summit block, then scramble south around the west side of a large summit boulder to the base of a short low-5th-class step that gains the true summit. An old fixed rappel anchor sits at the top for the descent. Most parties do it as a long day from the Washington Pass pullout, and many combine it with the neighboring Acropolis and Niki Tower to the south for an efficient multi-summit day on the ridge.

This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. The route involves approximately 9-10 miles of approach hiking, making it a typical 2-day backpacking objective. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.
before.approach: Drive Highway 101 to Sequim Bay State Park area, turn left on Louella Road for 1 mile, then left on Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles (it becomes FS Road 28 at the Forest Boundary), then turn right onto FS Road 2880, drive past Dungeness Forks Campground for 1 mile, stay left onto FS Road 2870 for 8.7 miles to Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Upper Dungeness Trail is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike the trail 3.4 miles and 600 feet to Camp Handy, then take the left fork and continue 3 miles and 1,850 feet to Boulder Camp (total: 6.4 miles, 2,450 feet gain). From Boulder Camp, continue south approximately 1.5-2 miles, crossing creeks, until you reach the final larger creek that flows from the cirque SE of Warrior Peak. Continue past this creek to a boulder field, then head up and back left toward the creek, staying under a band of cliffs, and continue up the boulders approximately 1 mile and 1,200 feet to reach the cirque at approximately 5,900 feet.

before.beta: A premier alpine testpiece featuring five pitches of high-quality granite climbing to the summit terrace, plus a short sixth pitch up an easy chimney to the summit. The route climbs splitter cracks and exposed face climbing over 600 vertical feet. Pitch 2 contains the crux with thin cracks, bulbous knobs, and a small roof. The climbing features varied terrain including incipient flakes, stemming, and lieback sections. Protection is generally reliable on white granite. The onsight first free ascent in 2007 was completed with no falls. Descent via four double-rope rappels from the summit.

Pick up the climbers' trail from the pullout, cross the basin and gain the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat. Follow the north ridge, which dips slightly in places, to the summit pyramid. There the rock opens into many possible lines; keeping to the north (right-hand) side is easier, and there are rappel slings on the far side. Expect loose rock and choose lines carefully.
before.approach: Park on the wide paved shoulder of SR-20 about three quarters of a mile west of the signed Blue Lake trailhead lot, on the north side, where there is no guard rail. A good climbers' trail leads from the road through forest into the basin. No pass is needed at the pullout; the Blue Lake lot needs a forest pass.

before.beta: From the col/notch behind the tower, cross a steep snowfield (ice axe recommended) to reach the base. The route climbs mostly Class 4 rock with a short Class 5 chimney partway up, on solid granite with good natural hand- and footholds, finishing with a friction-face section to the summit.
Follows the obvious long fingercrack layback corner on a buttress near Ellation. Chain anchor at the top. Often combined with Blood Orgy (rappel or downclimb between the two).

4-pitch trad climbing route graded 5.11a/b (also 6c/23/VIII-/E3 in other systems). Granite climbing on Cutthroat Creek Wall. From parking, hike approximately 1/4 mile on old roadbed, look for cairns marking left turn uphill. Bushwhack through woods with no trail, gaining elevation quickly. Traverse leftward in open forest and on slabby benches to reach shoulder at base of wall's right-hand side. Expect lichen and loose rock (first climbed in 2009 and seldom repeated). Trad protection: doubles to a #3 Camalot, weighted toward small cams and wires, with RPs for thin seams. Early season may have snow/ice hazards. Rock is granite of good quality.
before.approach: From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 for approximately 28 miles (4.5 miles east of Washington Pass). Turn right on Forest Service Road 400 and follow for 1 mile to the trailhead parking area on the left side of the road.

before.beta: Zool Patch starts up double cracks just left of Clean Break, climbs a 5.9 offwidth flake on pitch 2, then trends left on a brushy, poorly protected traverse across blank slabs (avoided rather than climbed directly) to a pair of bail trees, from which two double-rope rappels return to the base.
Meander up the smooth surface right of the arete, clipping one bolt, then a pin, then two more bolts. A few nuts and small cams add security.
